topics.name: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
topics.summary: The d-block spans groups 3–12 and comprises four transition series: 3d (Sc–Zn), 4d (Y–Cd), 5d (La/Hf–Hg) and the incomplete 6d series. A transition element is defined as one whose atom, or a common ion it forms, has a partially filled (n−1)d subshell. This excludes Zn, Cd and Hg, whose atoms and ions carry a completed d<sup>10</sup> shell, so they are classed as d-block but not typical transition elements. The general outer configuration is (n−1)d<sup>1–10</sup>ns<sup>0–2</sup>, but extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled d subshells causes irregular configurations at Cr ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>) and Cu ([Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>) in the 3d series, with similar anomalies recurring among the 4d and 5d metals (e.g. Pd, Ag, Au). The f-block holds the lanthanoids (Ce–Lu, filling 4f) and actinoids (Th–Lr, filling 5f); La and Ac, though technically d-block, are conventionally grouped with the f-block as the reference elements of each series.
key_formulas: General d-block configuration: (n−1)d<sup>1–10</sup>ns<sup>0–2</sup>
General f-block configuration: (n−2)f<sup>1–14</sup>(n−1)d<sup>0–1</sup>ns<sup>2</sup>
Cr: [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>; Cu: [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> (half-filled/fully-filled stability)
topics.worked_example: Write the electronic configuration of Mn (Z=25) and state whether it is a typical transition element. Filling order gives [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>. Since the 3d subshell is partially filled (5 of 10 electrons) in the atom itself, Mn is a typical transition element; its common Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>) also retains a partially filled d subshell, reinforcing this classification.
common_mistakes: Assuming Zn, Cd and Hg are typical transition elements simply because they sit in the d-block, ignoring their filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration
Writing Cr as [Ar]3d<sup>4</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> and Cu as [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> instead of the stability-driven [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> and [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>
Forgetting to check the configuration of the common ion (not just the neutral atom) when deciding if an element is a transition element

topics.name: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
topics.summary: Across a transition series, atomic radii fall steadily at first as increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud inward, but the fall flattens and even reverses slightly near the end of the series because added d-electrons repel each other and partially offset the rising nuclear charge. Comparing series, 4d atoms are noticeably larger than 3d atoms, but 5d atoms are close in size to 4d atoms rather than larger – this near-identity is a direct consequence of the lanthanoid contraction preceding the 5d series, which causes pairs such as Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta to have almost indistinguishable radii and very similar chemistry. All d-block elements are metals, showing typical metallic properties (lustre, high tensile strength, good thermal/electrical conductivity, malleability, ductility, and formation of alloys). Metallic character stays essentially unchanged across a series, though enthalpies of atomisation are very high compared with s- and p-block metals because both ns and (n−1)d electrons participate in metallic bonding.
key_formulas: Radius trend within a series: decreases initially, then levels off/rises slightly near group 11–12
Radius comparison across series: r(3d) < r(4d) ≈ r(5d) (lanthanoid contraction effect)
topics.worked_example: Explain why Zr (r ≈ 160 pm) and Hf (r ≈ 159 pm) have almost identical atomic radii despite Hf lying one full period below Zr. Normally an increase in principal quantum number would make Hf noticeably larger. However, the 14 lanthanoids inserted between La and Hf cause a steady lanthanoid contraction that almost exactly cancels the expected size increase, leaving Zr and Hf nearly the same size and chemically very similar, which historically made them difficult to separate.
common_mistakes: Assuming atomic radius decreases smoothly and continuously across the entire transition series with no levelling off
Expecting 5d elements to always be larger than their 4d counterparts, overlooking the lanthanoid contraction
Confusing 'metallic character stays roughly constant' with 'metallic character decreases sharply', unlike the trend across p-block periods

topics.name: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
topics.summary: First ionization enthalpies of the 3d transition metals rise only gradually and irregularly across the series, unlike the sharper rise seen in a p-block period, because electrons are being removed from an inner (n−1)d subshell whose shielding is inconsistent. Elements with extra-stable half-filled (d<sup>5</sup>) or fully-filled (d<sup>10</sup>) configurations, such as Cr and Zn relative to their neighbours, show small deviations from the smooth trend. A defining feature of transition metals is their variable oxidation states, arising because the energies of (n−1)d and ns electrons are very close, so both sets can be involved in bonding. Early in the 3d series the maximum oxidation state rises with the number of unpaired d and s electrons, peaking at +7 for Mn (3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>); beyond Mn, the higher oxidation states become progressively less stable because the d-electrons are held more tightly by the increasing nuclear charge, and +2/+3 states dominate towards the end of the series.
key_formulas: Maximum oxidation state (early 3d series) ≈ total number of 3d + 4s electrons available for bonding
Highest common oxidation state in the 3d series: Mn = +7 (in KMnO<sub>4</sub>)
topics.worked_example: Predict the highest oxidation state shown by Mn and justify it from its configuration. Mn is [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, giving 7 electrons beyond the argon core. When all 7 are formally involved in bonding, as in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (permanganate), Mn attains its maximum oxidation state of +7, matching the group number reached by summing 3d and 4s electrons.
common_mistakes: Expecting ionization enthalpy to rise as smoothly across a transition series as it does across a p-block period
Assuming every transition metal reaches an oxidation state equal to its group number, when stability actually falls off sharply after Mn
Forgetting that +2 is a common oxidation state for almost all 3d metals because it corresponds to loss of just the two 4s electrons

topics.name: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
topics.summary: Standard electrode potentials (E°, M<sup>2+</sup>/M) for the 3d metals are mostly negative, reflecting their general reactivity, but the trend across the series is irregular rather than smooth because it depends on a combination of the enthalpy of atomisation, the sum of ionization enthalpies, and the hydration enthalpy of the resulting ion. Mn and Zn show more negative E° values than expected from position alone because losing electrons to form Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) or Zn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>10</sup>) gives an especially stable configuration, making oxidation of the metal comparatively easy. Copper is the notable exception with a positive E° (Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu = +0.34 V), so copper does not displace hydrogen from dilute non-oxidizing acids such as HCl or dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; it dissolves only in oxidizing acids like hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or HNO<sub>3</sub>, where the acid's anion, not H<sup>+</sup>, is reduced. This reactivity pattern underlies which transition metals are attacked by dilute acids and which require oxidizing conditions.
key_formulas: E°(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V (positive → Cu does not liberate H<sub>2</sub> from dilute acids)
E° trend depends on: Δ<sub>a</sub>H (atomisation) + ΣIE (ionization) + Δ<sub>hyd</sub>H (hydration)
topics.worked_example: Explain why copper metal does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid but does dissolve in hot concentrated nitric acid. Cu has a positive standard reduction potential (+0.34 V for Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu), meaning Cu<sup>2+</sup> is more easily reduced than H<sup>+</sup>, so the reverse reaction (Cu being oxidised by H<sup>+</sup>) is not spontaneous. Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> instead oxidises Cu using the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ion (reduced to NO<sub>2</sub> or NO), which has a more favourable reduction potential than H<sup>+</sup>, so the reaction proceeds.
common_mistakes: Assuming all transition metals liberate H<sub>2</sub> gas readily from dilute acids like the alkali/alkaline earth metals do
Treating the E° trend across the 3d series as a smooth, monotonic curve rather than one shaped by three competing enthalpy terms
Overlooking that Mn and Zn owe their unusually negative E° values to the extra stability of d<sup>5</sup> and d<sup>10</sup> ions, not to any simple positional trend

topics.name: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
topics.summary: Most transition metal ions are paramagnetic because they contain unpaired electrons in the (n−1)d subshell; the magnetic moment can be estimated from the spin-only formula μ = √n(n+2) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Ions with d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> configurations (e.g. Sc<sup>3+</sup>, Ti<sup>4+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>+</sup>) have no unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic. Colour in transition metal compounds arises mainly from d-d transitions, in which an electron absorbs visible light to jump between split d orbitals; consequently, ions with no d electrons or a completely filled d<sup>10</sup> shell are typically colourless (Sc<sup>3+</sup>, Ti<sup>4+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>+</sup>), while partially filled configurations (Ti<sup>3+</sup>, V<sup>3+</sup>, Mn<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>2+</sup>, etc.) are coloured. Transition metals and their compounds are widely used as catalysts because of their ability to adopt variable oxidation states and to form unstable intermediate species with reactants, lowering the activation energy; examples include Fe<sup>3+</sup> in the iodide–persulphate reaction, V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> in the Contact process, finely divided Ni in hydrogenation, and TiCl<sub>4</sub> in Ziegler–Natta polymerisation.
key_formulas: Spin-only magnetic moment: μ = √n(n+2) BM, n = number of unpaired electrons
d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> → diamagnetic and (usually) colourless
topics.worked_example: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Mn<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>5</sup>) and state whether it is coloured. All 5 d-electrons are unpaired (high-spin d<sup>5</sup>), so n = 5 and μ = √5(5+2) = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM, making Mn<sup>2+</sup> strongly paramagnetic. Since it has a partially filled d subshell, d-d transitions are possible, but they are Laporde- and spin-forbidden, so Mn<sup>2+</sup> solutions are only very faintly pink rather than intensely coloured.
common_mistakes: Assuming every transition metal ion must be coloured, forgetting that d<sup>0</sup> and d<sup>10</sup> ions are colourless
Using the total number of d electrons instead of the number of unpaired d electrons in the spin-only formula
Thinking a catalyst is consumed permanently in the reaction, rather than being regenerated after forming a temporary intermediate

topics.name: Alloy Formation & Interstitial Compounds
topics.summary: Transition metals readily form alloys with one another because their atomic sizes are similar enough that atoms of one metal can substitute for atoms of another in the crystal lattice without excessive distortion. The resulting alloys are typically harder and have higher melting points than the constituent metals, since the interlocking of atoms of different sizes hinders slip along crystal planes; well-known examples include brass (Cu–Zn), bronze (Cu–Sn), stainless steel (Fe–Cr–Ni–C) and nichrome (Ni–Cr) used in heating elements. In interstitial compounds, by contrast, small non-metal atoms such as H, C, N or B are trapped in the octahedral or tetrahedral voids of a transition metal's close-packed lattice rather than replacing metal atoms. These compounds (e.g. TiC, Fe<sub>3</sub>N, VN, TiH<sub>1.7</sub>) are typically hard, have high melting points close to those of the parent metal, retain metallic conductivity, and are chemically fairly inert, which is why interstitial carbides and nitrides are valued for cutting tools and wear-resistant coatings.
key_formulas: Alloy: substitutional mixing of similarly-sized metal atoms in a lattice (e.g. brass = Cu + Zn)
Interstitial compound: small atoms (H, C, N, B) occupy voids of a metal lattice without replacing metal atoms
topics.worked_example: Explain why stainless steel is much harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure iron. Stainless steel is an alloy of Fe with Cr, Ni and a small amount of C. The Cr and Ni atoms, being similar in size to Fe, substitute into the iron lattice and disrupt regular slip planes, increasing hardness, while chromium forms a thin, adherent, self-healing oxide layer (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) on the surface that protects the underlying metal from further corrosion, unlike pure iron which rusts readily.
common_mistakes: Confusing an interstitial compound (small non-metal atoms in lattice voids) with a substitutional alloy (similarly sized metal atoms replacing each other)
Assuming alloys are always weaker than their pure constituent metals, when in fact they are usually harder
Believing interstitial carbides/nitrides lose metallic conductivity because a non-metal has been incorporated

topics.name: Potassium Dichromate & Potassium Permanganate – Preparation, Properties & Reactions
topics.summary: Potassium dichromate is manufactured from chromite ore (FeCr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), which is fused with sodium carbonate in air to give sodium chromate; this is acidified to sodium dichromate, which is then treated with KCl to crystallise out the less soluble potassium dichromate. In aqueous solution, yellow chromate (CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>) and orange dichromate (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>) exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium, with chromate favoured in alkaline medium and dichromate in acidic medium. Dichromate is a powerful oxidising agent in acidic solution, oxidising Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, I<sup>−</sup> to I<sub>2</sub>, and SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> to SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, being itself reduced to green Cr<sup>3+</sup>. Potassium permanganate is manufactured from pyrolusite (MnO<sub>2</sub>), fused with KOH and an oxidant (KNO<sub>3</sub> or air) to give green potassium manganate (K<sub>2</sub>MnO<sub>4</sub>), which is oxidised electrolytically or with Cl<sub>2</sub>/O<sub>3</sub> to deep purple KMnO<sub>4</sub>. KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises differently depending on medium: to colourless Mn<sup>2+</sup> in acidic solution, to brown MnO<sub>2</sub> in neutral or faintly alkaline solution, and to green MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> in strongly alkaline solution.
key_formulas: 2CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O (acidic medium favours dichromate)
MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 5e<sup>−</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (acidic reduction of permanganate)
topics.worked_example: Explain what happens when a few drops of NaOH are added to an orange aqueous solution of potassium dichromate. Adding alkali raises the pH and shifts the chromate–dichromate equilibrium (2CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> ⇌ Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O) to the left, converting orange dichromate ions into yellow chromate ions; the colour change from orange to yellow is a classic qualitative test for this equilibrium.
common_mistakes: Believing chromate and dichromate are entirely separate, non-interconvertible compounds rather than pH-dependent forms of the same equilibrium
Writing the reduction product of KMnO<sub>4</sub> in acidic medium as MnO<sub>2</sub> instead of the correct colourless Mn<sup>2+</sup>
Forgetting that the oxidising strength and reduction product of KMnO<sub>4</sub> both change with the pH of the medium

topics.name: Lanthanoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Lanthanoid Contraction
topics.summary: Lanthanoids (Ce–Lu) have the general configuration [Xe]4f<sup>1–14</sup>5d<sup>0–1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>, and almost all show +3 as their most stable and characteristic oxidation state, since this leaves behind particularly stable f<sup>0</sup>, f<sup>7</sup> or f<sup>14</sup> arrangements for certain ions. A few lanthanoids also display +2 or +4 states when doing so attains or approaches one of these stable configurations: Ce<sup>4+</sup> (f<sup>0</sup>) is a mild oxidising agent, while Eu<sup>2+</sup> (f<sup>7</sup>) and Yb<sup>2+</sup> (f<sup>14</sup>) are reducing. A defining feature of the series is the lanthanoid contraction: a slow but steady fall in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu, caused by the poor shielding one 4f electron provides for another, so effective nuclear charge rises steadily across the series. The cumulative contraction over 14 elements is large enough that it nearly cancels the size increase expected on descending from the 4d to the 5d series, making pairs like Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta almost identical in radius and chemical behaviour and making the lanthanoids themselves difficult to separate from one another.
key_formulas: General lanthanoid configuration: [Xe]4f<sup>1–14</sup>5d<sup>0–1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>
Extra-stable f configurations: f<sup>0</sup> (Ce<sup>4+</sup>), f<sup>7</sup> (Eu<sup>2+</sup>, Gd<sup>3+</sup>), f<sup>14</sup> (Yb<sup>2+</sup>, Lu<sup>3+</sup>)
topics.worked_example: Explain why Ce<sup>4+</sup> is a good oxidising agent in aqueous solution even though +3 is the typical lanthanoid oxidation state. Ce is [Xe]4f<sup>1</sup>5d<sup>1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>; losing all four outer electrons to form Ce<sup>4+</sup> empties the 4f subshell completely, giving the extra stability of an f<sup>0</sup> configuration. This makes the +4 state accessible for Ce specifically, and Ce<sup>4+</sup> readily gains an electron to revert to the more typical, very stable Ce<sup>3+</sup>, which is why it behaves as an oxidising agent.
common_mistakes: Assuming every lanthanoid can show +2 and +4 states as freely as +3, when these are limited to specific elements with a stability-driving reason
Attributing the near-identical radii of Zr/Hf or Nb/Ta to random coincidence rather than to the lanthanoid contraction that precedes the 5d series
Confusing lanthanoid contraction (a steady, cumulative decrease in radius across 14 elements) with a single large drop between two adjacent elements

topics.name: Actinoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Comparison with Lanthanoids
topics.summary: Actinoids (Th–Lr) have the general configuration [Rn]5f<sup>0–14</sup>6d<sup>0–2</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>, but because the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie unusually close in energy, their electronic configurations are less regular and harder to predict than those of the lanthanoids. All actinoids are radioactive, and this instability increases sharply for elements beyond uranium (the transuranium elements), most of which are synthetic and have very short half-lives. Like the lanthanoids, +3 is a common and often most stable oxidation state late in the series, but early actinoids show a much wider range of oxidation states than early lanthanoids – for example uranium commonly shows +3 to +6 and neptunium, plutonium and americium can reach +7 – because the comparable energies of 5f, 6d and 7s electrons allow more of them to participate in bonding. An actinoid contraction parallel to the lanthanoid contraction also occurs, and is in fact somewhat greater across the series because 5f electrons shield each other even less effectively than 4f electrons do. Actinoid compounds also tend to be more strongly coloured and more prone to forming complexes than their lanthanoid analogues.
key_formulas: General actinoid configuration: [Rn]5f<sup>0–14</sup>6d<sup>0–2</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>
Actinoid contraction > lanthanoid contraction per element (poorer 5f shielding than 4f shielding)
topics.worked_example: Explain why uranium shows a much wider range of oxidation states (+3 to +6) than a typical lanthanoid such as neodymium, which is almost always +3. In uranium, the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close enough in energy that electrons from more than one subshell can be removed with comparable ease, allowing several oxidation states to form with reasonable stability. In lanthanoids, the 4f orbitals lie much lower in energy and are shielded from bonding by the filled 5s and 5p subshells, so lanthanoid chemistry is dominated almost entirely by the +3 state.
common_mistakes: Assuming actinoids behave exactly like lanthanoids simply because both are f-block series with a dominant +3 state
Forgetting that actinoids are all radioactive, while among lanthanoids only promethium is radioactive
Underestimating how much closer 5f, 6d and 7s energies are compared to 4f, 5d and 6s, which is the real reason for the actinoids' irregular configurations and wider oxidation-state range

topics.name: Applications of d- & f-Block Elements
topics.summary: The d- and f-block elements underpin a wide range of industrial and everyday applications. Iron, chromium, manganese, nickel and vanadium are the backbone of the steel and alloy industry, giving products such as stainless steel and high-speed tool steel their strength and corrosion resistance. Many transition metals and their compounds serve as catalysts: iron and molybdenum in the Haber process for ammonia, vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process for sulphuric acid, finely divided nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils, and titanium tetrachloride with an aluminium alkyl (Ziegler–Natta catalyst) in the polymerisation of alkenes. Potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate are widely used oxidising agents in volumetric titrations, in the tanning of leather (chromium salts), and as disinfectants or oxidisers in organic synthesis. Among the f-block elements, mischmetal (a lanthanoid-rich alloy) is used in lighter flints and as a deoxidiser in metallurgy, cerium(IV) oxide is used for glass polishing, and neodymium compounds are used in powerful permanent magnets; uranium and plutonium fuel nuclear reactors, while artificially produced radioisotopes of some d-block elements (such as cobalt-60) are used in radiotherapy.
key_formulas: Haber process catalyst: Fe (promoted with Mo); Contact process catalyst: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>
Ziegler–Natta catalyst: TiCl<sub>4</sub> + Al(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>
topics.worked_example: Identify the catalyst used in the Contact process for manufacturing sulphuric acid and state the reaction it catalyses. Vanadium(V) oxide (V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) is used to catalyse the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub> (2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub>), the key step before SO<sub>3</sub> is absorbed to eventually form H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> works by cycling between V<sup>5+</sup> and V<sup>4+</sup> oxidation states.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which transition metal catalyses which industrial process (e.g. confusing the Haber process catalyst with the Contact process catalyst)
Assuming lanthanoid/actinoid applications are purely nuclear, overlooking everyday uses like lighter flints, glass polishing and permanent magnets
Forgetting that a catalyst such as V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> works by cycling through more than one oxidation state rather than staying chemically unchanged throughout

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Which of these elements has a completely filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration in both its atom and its common +2 ion, and is therefore excluded from the typical transition elements?
options: Fe
Zn
Cu
Sc
questions.explanation: Zn is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, so both the atom and the ion have a fully filled d subshell, which is why zinc is classed as d-block but not a typical transition element.
questions.hint: Look for the element whose d subshell stays completely full even after it forms its common ion.
distractor_logic: Fe is [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> with a partially filled d subshell, so it is a typical transition element, not one excluded on these grounds.
Cu atom is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>, but its common Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion is 3d<sup>9</sup> (partially filled), so copper still counts as a typical transition element.

Sc is [Ar]3d<sup>1</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> with a partially filled d subshell in the atom; it is excluded for a different reason (its only common ion, Sc<sup>3+</sup>, is d<sup>0</sup>), not for a filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Which configuration correctly represents chromium (Z=24), accounting for the extra stability of a half-filled subshell?
options: [Ar]3d<sup>4</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>
[Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>
[Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>0</sup>
[Ar]3d<sup>3</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>4p<sup>1</sup>
questions.explanation: One 4s electron shifts into the 3d subshell so that chromium attains the extra-stable half-filled arrangement [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> instead of the naive aufbau prediction.
questions.hint: Chromium is a classic exception to straightforward aufbau filling.
distractor_logic: This follows the aufbau order strictly for 24 electrons but ignores the extra stability gained by a half-filled 3d subshell, which is what actually happens.
This transfers both 4s electrons into 3d, overcorrecting; only one 4s electron moves to reach the more stable half-filled 3d<sup>5</sup> arrangement.
This places an electron in the 4p subshell before 3d and 4s are filled, violating the normal filling order for period 4.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Which range of elements correctly constitutes the second (4d) transition series?
options: Sc to Zn
Y to Cd
La to Hg
Ce to Lu
questions.explanation: The second transition series fills the 4d subshell, running from Y (Z=39) to Cd (Z=48).
questions.hint: This series lies directly below the first (3d) series in the periodic table.
distractor_logic: This is the range of the first (3d) transition series, not the second.
This range spans the third (5d) transition series together with lanthanum, not the second series.
This range corresponds to the lanthanoids (f-block), not a d-block transition series.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Which pair of elements is conventionally grouped with the f-block as the first ('reference') member of the lanthanoid and actinoid rows, even though each technically belongs to the d-block?
options: Ce and Th
La and Ac
Lu and Lr
Sc and Y
questions.explanation: La ([Xe]5d<sup>1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>) and Ac ([Rn]6d<sup>1</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>) have no f electrons themselves but are placed at the head of the lanthanoid and actinoid rows by convention.
questions.hint: These two elements have zero electrons in the f subshell, yet give their names to the whole f-block series.
distractor_logic: Ce and Th are the first true f-block elements (with 4f and 5f electrons appearing), not the borderline d-block elements placed alongside them for convenience.
Lu and Lr are the last members of the lanthanoid and actinoid rows, not the elements placed at the start.
Sc and Y are ordinary 3d/4d transition elements and have no special connection to f-block placement.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Which trend best describes atomic radii across a typical 3d transition series, from left to right?
options: They decrease steadily, then flatten out with a slight rise near the end
They increase steadily throughout
They decrease and then rise sharply beyond group 12
They remain completely constant throughout
questions.explanation: Radii shrink as nuclear charge rises across the series, but electron-electron repulsion among added d-electrons slows and slightly reverses this fall near groups 11-12.
questions.hint: The fall in size isn't uniform all the way across the row.
distractor_logic: Radii generally fall due to rising nuclear charge; a steady increase across the whole series does not match the observed trend.
The rise near the end is only slight and gradual, not a sharp jump beyond group 12.
Radii do change measurably across the series, so 'completely constant' is incorrect.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Zr and Hf show almost identical atomic radii mainly because of:
options: Similar nuclear charge
The lanthanoid contraction
Both being liquids at room temperature
Identical electron affinity
questions.explanation: The steady contraction across the 14 lanthanoids inserted before Hf nearly cancels the size increase expected from an added principal quantum shell, leaving Zr and Hf almost the same size.
questions.hint: Something happens between La and Hf in the periodic table that offsets the usual increase in size down a group.
distractor_logic: Nuclear charge actually differs considerably between Zr and Hf; charge alone would predict a size difference, not similarity.
Neither element's physical state at room temperature has any bearing on atomic radius.
Electron affinity is a separate periodic property and does not explain their near-identical radii.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical property of d-block metals?
options: High melting and boiling points
Good electrical and thermal conductivity
Low enthalpy of atomisation compared to s-block metals
Formation of alloys with other metals
questions.explanation: Transition metals actually have unusually HIGH enthalpies of atomisation compared to s-block metals, since both ns and (n-1)d electrons contribute to strong metallic bonding, so this statement is false and is the exception being asked for.
questions.hint: Three of these are genuine transition-metal traits; one describes the opposite of what is actually observed.
distractor_logic: High melting and boiling points are indeed characteristic of transition metals, so this IS typical and not the answer being sought.
Good conductivity is indeed a genuine transition-metal property, so this is not the exception.
Alloy formation is indeed common among transition metals, so this is not the exception.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Metallic character across a 3d transition series, compared with the sharp change seen across a p-block period, is best described as:
options: Sharply decreasing left to right
Remaining metallic throughout with little change
Changing from metal to non-metal
Increasing sharply toward group 12
questions.explanation: Unlike a p-block period where character shifts from metal to non-metal, every 3d element from Sc to Zn remains a metal, so metallic character changes only slightly across the series.
questions.hint: Think about whether any 3d element is a non-metal.
distractor_logic: There is no sharp decrease in metallic character across the series; all members remain metals.
No 3d element becomes a non-metal, so this description is incorrect.
Metallic character does not increase sharply toward the end of the series; it stays broadly similar.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: Which 3d metal shows the highest common oxidation state within the series?
options: Sc
Cr
Mn
Zn
questions.explanation: Mn ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>) can use all 7 outer electrons in bonding, reaching a maximum oxidation state of +7, as in KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
questions.hint: This element has 7 electrons beyond the argon core available for bonding.
distractor_logic: Sc's highest common oxidation state is only +3.
Cr commonly reaches +6, one less than Mn's maximum of +7.
Zn is essentially restricted to +2 owing to its stable, fully-filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: The relatively small and irregular increase in first ionization enthalpy across a 3d transition series (compared to a typical p-block period) mainly occurs because:
options: Electrons are removed from an inner, inconsistently shielding d subshell
Transition metals have no core electrons
Nuclear charge decreases across the series
All 3d metals have identical atomic radii
questions.explanation: Because the (n-1)d electrons being removed shield each other unevenly, the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons rises unevenly, giving a gentler, irregular ionization-enthalpy trend.
questions.hint: Focus on where the electron being removed actually comes from.
distractor_logic: Transition metals do have core electrons; this statement is simply false.
Nuclear charge increases, not decreases, across a period as protons are added.
Atomic radii are not identical across the series; they vary, just not smoothly.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: Which oxidation state is most widely and commonly shown by nearly all the 3d transition metals?
questions.explanation: +2 corresponds to loss of just the two outer 4s electrons and is the most broadly common oxidation state across the 3d series.
questions.hint: Think about which state simply requires losing the outermost s electrons.
distractor_logic: +1 is rare among the 3d metals, notably seen for Cu(I) but not as a general series-wide state.
+5 is accessible to only a few early metals such as V, not a widely common state.
+7 is essentially unique to Mn among the 3d metals.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: The extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled d subshells causes a notable deviation in electronic configuration at which pair of 3d elements?
options: Sc and Ti
Cr and Cu
Mn and Fe
Fe and Ni
questions.explanation: Cr ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>) and Cu ([Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>) both deviate from the simple aufbau prediction to attain a half-filled or fully-filled 3d subshell.
questions.hint: One of these elements ends up with a half-filled d subshell, the other with a fully-filled one.
distractor_logic: Sc and Ti follow the expected filling order without any such special deviation.
Mn and Fe follow the normal, non-anomalous filling pattern for their electron counts.
Fe and Ni also have ordinary, non-anomalous d-electron counts (d<sup>6</sup> and d<sup>8</sup>) and show no such deviation.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Which 3d metal has a positive standard electrode potential (M<sup>2+</sup>/M) and therefore does not liberate hydrogen from dilute non-oxidizing acids?
options: Fe
Zn
Cu
Mn
questions.explanation: Cu has E°(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V, a positive value, so H<sup>+</sup> cannot oxidise Cu metal in dilute non-oxidizing acids.
questions.hint: This is the classic exception among common 3d metals when it comes to reacting with dilute acids.
distractor_logic: Fe has a negative E° and reacts with dilute acids to release H<sub>2</sub>.
Zn has a strongly negative E° and readily displaces H<sub>2</sub> from dilute acids.
Mn has a very negative E° due to the stability of Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) and reacts readily with dilute acids.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Copper dissolves in hot concentrated nitric acid mainly because:
options: Cu has a very negative electrode potential
The NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ion, not H<sup>+</sup>, is reduced by Cu
Cu reacts violently with any acid
Nitric acid contains no oxidizing anion
questions.explanation: Since Cu will not reduce H<sup>+</sup>, dissolution instead proceeds via reduction of the oxidizing NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ion to NO or NO<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Ask which species in nitric acid is actually capable of oxidising copper.
distractor_logic: Cu's electrode potential is positive, not very negative, which is precisely why it can't reduce H<sup>+</sup>.
Cu does not react with dilute non-oxidizing acids at all, so 'any acid' is incorrect.
Nitric acid's NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ion is exactly the oxidizing anion responsible for dissolving copper.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Mn shows an unusually negative standard electrode potential mainly because:
options: Mn<sup>2+</sup> has a fully-filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration
Mn<sup>2+</sup> has an extra-stable half-filled d<sup>5</sup> configuration
Mn has the largest atomic radius in the 3d series
Mn is not a transition element
questions.explanation: Forming the extra-stable half-filled d<sup>5</sup> Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion is comparatively easy, making oxidation of Mn metal favourable and giving a very negative electrode potential.
questions.hint: Think about how many d electrons remain once Mn loses its two 4s electrons.
distractor_logic: Mn<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>5</sup>, not d<sup>10</sup>; the fully-filled configuration belongs to ions like Zn<sup>2+</sup>.
Mn does not have the largest radius in the series; its radius is unexceptional.
Mn is very much a typical transition element, with a partially filled d subshell in its common ions.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Which set correctly lists the three main factors that together determine a transition metal's standard electrode potential?
options: Atomic colour, catalytic activity, magnetism
Enthalpy of atomisation, ionization enthalpy, hydration enthalpy
Melting point, density, hardness
Alloy-forming ability, radius, oxidation state
questions.explanation: Electrode potential reflects an energy cycle combining the enthalpy of atomisation of the metal, its ionization enthalpy, and the hydration enthalpy of the resulting ion.
questions.hint: Think of the Born-Haber-type cycle used to rationalise E° values.
distractor_logic: Colour, catalytic activity and magnetism are unrelated to the thermodynamic cycle that determines E°.
Melting point, density and hardness are physical properties not directly part of the electrode-potential energy cycle.
Alloy-forming ability and radius are not the specific enthalpy terms used to rationalise E° trends.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: Which ion is diamagnetic due to a fully-filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration?
options: Fe<sup>2+</sup>
Zn<sup>2+</sup>
Mn<sup>2+</sup>
Cu<sup>2+</sup>
questions.explanation: Zn<sup>2+</sup> is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, with all d electrons paired, making it diamagnetic.
questions.hint: Look for the ion with no unpaired d electrons at all.
distractor_logic: Fe<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>6</sup> and typically has unpaired electrons, making it paramagnetic.
Mn<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>5</sup> with five unpaired electrons, strongly paramagnetic.
Cu<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>9</sup> with one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic, not diamagnetic.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: The spin-only formula used to estimate the magnetic moment of a transition metal ion is:
options: μ = √n(n+2) BM
μ = √n/(n+2)
μ = 2√n BM
questions.explanation: The spin-only magnetic moment is μ = √n(n+2) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
questions.hint: The correct expression involves a square root of a product, not the product itself.
distractor_logic: This omits the required square root over the product n(n+2).
This incorrectly uses a quotient (n divided by (n+2)) instead of the product n(n+2).
This uses an unrelated expression, 2√n, that does not correspond to the spin-only formula.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: Colour in most transition metal compounds arises mainly from:
options: s-s electron transitions
d-d electron transitions
Nuclear transitions
p-p electron transitions
questions.explanation: Partially filled d orbitals split in energy in the presence of ligands, allowing electrons to absorb visible light and transition between them, producing colour.
questions.hint: Think about which subshell is partially filled in coloured transition metal ions.
distractor_logic: s orbitals are not split or partially filled in a way that produces visible-light absorption of this kind.
Nuclear transitions involve far higher energies (gamma-ray region) and are unrelated to visible colour.
p orbitals are not the partially filled subshell responsible for transition-metal colour.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: Transition metals are effective catalysts largely because of their ability to:
options: Remain in a single fixed oxidation state
Show variable oxidation states and form intermediate complexes with reactants
Exist only as colourless ions
Resist forming any bond with reactant molecules
questions.explanation: Switching between accessible oxidation states lets transition metals form temporary intermediates with reactants, providing an alternative, lower-energy reaction pathway.
questions.hint: Catalytic ability is closely tied to a property discussed earlier in this chapter regarding multiple oxidation states.
distractor_logic: A single fixed oxidation state would prevent the intermediate-forming behaviour that makes these metals good catalysts.
Whether the ion is colourless has no bearing on catalytic ability.
Catalysis specifically requires forming (weak, temporary) bonds with reactants, not resisting them.

questions.topic: Alloy Formation & Interstitial Compounds
questions.question: Brass is an alloy of which two metals?
options: Cu and Sn
Cu and Zn
Fe and Cr
Ni and Cr
questions.explanation: Brass is a copper-zinc alloy, prized for its workability and golden appearance.
questions.hint: This alloy gives fittings and musical instruments their bright golden-yellow colour.
distractor_logic: Cu and Sn together form bronze, not brass.
Fe and Cr are components of stainless steel, not brass.
Ni and Cr together form nichrome, used in heating elements, not brass.

questions.topic: Alloy Formation & Interstitial Compounds
questions.question: In an interstitial compound such as TiC, the small carbon atoms are located:
options: Substituting for Ti atoms in the lattice
In the voids between the metal atoms of the lattice
Only on the outer surface of the metal
Dissolved as a separate liquid phase
questions.explanation: Interstitial compounds form when small atoms like C, N, H or B occupy the octahedral or tetrahedral voids within a metal's close-packed lattice.
questions.hint: The carbon atoms don't replace metal atoms; they slot in between them.
distractor_logic: Substitution of metal atoms describes an alloy, not an interstitial compound.
Interstitial atoms are distributed throughout the lattice, not confined to the surface.
TiC is a solid crystalline compound, not a mixture with a separate liquid phase.

questions.topic: Alloy Formation & Interstitial Compounds
questions.question: Which property is typical of interstitial compounds such as VN and Fe<sub>3</sub>N?
options: Low melting point and poor electrical conductivity
High melting point, hardness, and retained metallic conductivity
Complete loss of metallic character
High solubility in water
questions.explanation: Interstitial compounds retain a metal-like lattice, so they stay hard, high-melting, and electrically conductive, while also being chemically fairly inert.
questions.hint: These compounds still behave a lot like the parent metal in several respects.
distractor_logic: Interstitial compounds actually have high melting points and good conductivity, the opposite of this description.
Metallic conductivity is retained, not lost, in interstitial compounds.
Interstitial compounds are chemically fairly inert and are not notably water-soluble.

questions.topic: Alloy Formation & Interstitial Compounds
questions.question: Alloy formation is favoured between two transition metals mainly because:
options: Their atomic radii are very different
Their atomic radii are similar enough for mutual substitution in the lattice
They are always radioactive
They never form a solid solution
questions.explanation: Similar atomic sizes allow one metal's atoms to substitute for another's without excessive lattice strain, favouring alloy formation.
questions.hint: Think about what makes it geometrically easy for one type of atom to fit into another's crystal lattice.
distractor_logic: Very different radii would make it geometrically difficult for one metal to substitute into the other's lattice, hindering alloy formation.
Radioactivity is unrelated to alloy formation between transition metals.
Transition metals do form solid solutions (alloys) with each other, contrary to this statement.

questions.topic: Potassium Dichromate & Potassium Permanganate – Preparation, Properties & Reactions
questions.question: Potassium dichromate is manufactured industrially starting from which ore?
options: Pyrolusite
Chromite (FeCr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)
Bauxite
Haematite
questions.explanation: Chromite ore is fused with sodium carbonate in air to give sodium chromate, the starting point for dichromate manufacture.
questions.hint: This ore contains iron and chromium together.
distractor_logic: Pyrolusite (MnO<sub>2</sub>) is the starting ore for potassium permanganate, not dichromate.
Bauxite is the ore used for aluminium extraction, unrelated to dichromate manufacture.
Haematite is an iron ore, not the source of chromium for dichromate.

questions.topic: Potassium Dichromate & Potassium Permanganate – Preparation, Properties & Reactions
questions.question: In alkaline solution, orange dichromate ions convert to:
options: Green Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions
Yellow chromate ions, CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>
Metallic chromium
Chromium trioxide, CrO<sub>3</sub>
questions.explanation: Raising the pH shifts the chromate-dichromate equilibrium toward yellow CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
questions.hint: Think of the classic orange-to-yellow colour change with added alkali.
distractor_logic: Green Cr<sup>3+</sup> forms only when dichromate acts as an oxidizing agent and is itself reduced, not simply from a pH change.
No reduction to metallic chromium occurs from a simple pH shift.
CrO<sub>3</sub> is a separate, more strongly acidic oxide, not the product of this equilibrium shift.

questions.topic: Potassium Dichromate & Potassium Permanganate – Preparation, Properties & Reactions
questions.question: Potassium permanganate is manufactured industrially starting from which ore?
options: Chromite
Pyrolusite (MnO<sub>2</sub>)
Siderite
Cassiterite
questions.explanation: Pyrolusite is fused with KOH and an oxidant to give green K<sub>2</sub>MnO<sub>4</sub>, which is later oxidised to purple KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
questions.hint: This ore is a manganese oxide.
distractor_logic: Chromite is the starting ore for potassium dichromate, not permanganate.
Siderite is an iron carbonate ore, unrelated to permanganate manufacture.
Cassiterite is a tin ore, unrelated to permanganate manufacture.

questions.topic: Potassium Dichromate & Potassium Permanganate – Preparation, Properties & Reactions
questions.question: In acidic medium, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is reduced to:
options: MnO<sub>2</sub>
Mn<sup>2+</sup>
MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>
Mn metal
questions.explanation: In acidic solution, permanganate is reduced all the way to the nearly colourless Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion.
questions.hint: Acidic medium gives the most complete reduction of the three common outcomes for permanganate.
distractor_logic: MnO<sub>2</sub> is the reduction product in neutral or faintly alkaline medium, not strongly acidic medium.
MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> (manganate) forms only in strongly alkaline medium.
Permanganate is not reduced all the way to the free metal under these conditions.

questions.topic: Lanthanoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Lanthanoid Contraction
questions.question: The most common and stable oxidation state shown by lanthanoids is:
questions.explanation: Nearly all lanthanoids show +3 as their principal, most stable oxidation state.
questions.hint: This is the oxidation state shared by essentially every lanthanoid.
distractor_logic: +2 is shown only by a few lanthanoids (e.g. Eu, Yb) under special stability conditions, not as the general state.
+4 is likewise limited to specific cases (e.g. Ce), not the general oxidation state.
+5 is not shown by lanthanoids at all.

questions.topic: Lanthanoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Lanthanoid Contraction
questions.question: Ce<sup>4+</sup> acts as a mild oxidising agent in solution mainly because:
options: Ce<sup>4+</sup> is more stable than Ce<sup>3+</sup>
Reduction to the common, more stable Ce<sup>3+</sup> state is thermodynamically favourable
Ce<sup>4+</sup> has a completely filled f<sup>14</sup> configuration
Lanthanoids cannot exist in the +4 state
questions.explanation: Ce<sup>3+</sup> is the far more typical and stable lanthanoid state, so Ce<sup>4+</sup> readily gains an electron to revert to it, behaving as an oxidising agent.
questions.hint: Think about which oxidation state cerium 'wants' to settle into.
distractor_logic: It is Ce<sup>3+</sup>, not Ce<sup>4+</sup>, that is the more stable state; this is precisely why Ce<sup>4+</sup> is oxidizing.
Ce<sup>4+</sup> has an empty f<sup>0</sup> configuration, not a filled f<sup>14</sup> one.
The +4 state is exactly what Ce does show, though only as a minor, less stable oxidation state.

questions.topic: Lanthanoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Lanthanoid Contraction
questions.question: Lanthanoid contraction refers to:
options: A sudden decrease in radius between La and Ce only
A steady, cumulative decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the lanthanoid series
A steady increase in radius across the lanthanoid series
Contraction of only the nucleus, not the electron cloud
questions.explanation: Poor shielding by 4f electrons causes effective nuclear charge, and hence contraction, to build up gradually across all 14 lanthanoids.
questions.hint: This effect accumulates over the whole series, not just between two neighbours.
distractor_logic: The contraction is gradual across the whole series, not a single sudden drop between two elements.
Radii decrease, not increase, across the lanthanoid series.
It is the overall (effective) atomic/ionic size that contracts due to electron shielding effects, not the nucleus itself.

questions.topic: Lanthanoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Lanthanoid Contraction
questions.question: Which of the following best represents the general electronic configuration of a lanthanoid element?
options: [Xe]4f<sup>1–14</sup>5d<sup>0–1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>
[Rn]5f<sup>1–14</sup>6d<sup>0–2</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>
[Ar]3d<sup>1–10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>
[Kr]4d<sup>1–10</sup>5s<sup>2</sup>
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell on a [Xe] core, giving the general form [Xe]4f<sup>1–14</sup>5d<sup>0–1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>.
questions.hint: The noble-gas core for this series is xenon, and the subshell being filled is 4f.
distractor_logic: This [Rn] core with 5f describes the actinoids, not the lanthanoids.
This [Ar] core with 3d describes the first transition series, not the f-block.
This [Kr] core with 4d describes the second transition series, not the lanthanoids.

questions.topic: Actinoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Comparison with Lanthanoids
questions.question: Which property is shared by all actinoids?
options: They are all colourless
They are all radioactive
They are all liquids at room temperature
None of them form complexes
questions.explanation: Every actinoid, from Th to Lr, is radioactive, unlike the lanthanoids where only promethium is.
questions.hint: This is the defining difference from the lanthanoid series regarding stability of the nucleus.
distractor_logic: Many actinoid compounds are actually strongly coloured, not colourless.
Actinoids are solids at room temperature, like other metals in the f-block.
Actinoids readily form complexes, often more so than lanthanoids.

questions.topic: Actinoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Comparison with Lanthanoids
questions.question: Compared with the lanthanoids, the actinoids show:
options: A narrower range of oxidation states
A wider range of oxidation states
No variation in oxidation state at all
Exclusively negative oxidation states
questions.explanation: Because 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie close in energy, actinoids such as U, Np, Pu and Am access a much wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
questions.hint: Think about how close in energy the relevant orbitals are for this series compared to the lanthanoids.
distractor_logic: The actinoid range is wider, not narrower, than that of the lanthanoids.
Actinoids show considerable variation in oxidation state, especially the early members.
Actinoids show positive oxidation states (e.g. +3 to +7), not exclusively negative ones.

questions.topic: Actinoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Comparison with Lanthanoids
questions.question: Which of the following best represents the general electronic configuration of an actinoid element?
options: [Xe]4f<sup>1–14</sup>5d<sup>0–1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>
[Rn]5f<sup>0–14</sup>6d<sup>0–2</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>
[Ar]3d<sup>1–10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>
[Kr]4d<sup>1–10</sup>5s<sup>1</sup>
questions.explanation: Actinoids fill the 5f subshell on a [Rn] core, giving the general form [Rn]5f<sup>0–14</sup>6d<sup>0–2</sup>7s<sup>2</sup>.
questions.hint: The noble-gas core for this series is radon, and the subshell being filled is 5f.
distractor_logic: This [Xe] core with 4f describes the lanthanoids, not the actinoids.
This [Ar] core with 3d describes the first transition series, not the f-block.
This [Kr] core with 4d describes the second transition series, not the actinoids.

questions.topic: Actinoids – Configuration, Oxidation States & Comparison with Lanthanoids
questions.question: Which actinoid is the most abundant naturally occurring member and is widely used as nuclear reactor fuel?
options: Plutonium
Uranium
Curium
Americium
questions.explanation: Uranium occurs naturally in appreciable amounts and is the primary fuel used in nuclear reactors.
questions.hint: This element's ore, pitchblende, is mined directly from the earth, unlike most other actinoids.
distractor_logic: Plutonium is mainly produced artificially in reactors rather than mined in large natural quantities.
Curium is a synthetic transuranium element with no significant natural abundance.
Americium is likewise a synthetic transuranium element, not a naturally abundant fuel source.

questions.topic: Applications of d- & f-Block Elements
questions.question: Which transition metal oxide is used as the catalyst in the Contact process for manufacturing sulphuric acid?
options: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>
MnO<sub>2</sub>
CuO
questions.explanation: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> catalyses the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub> by cycling between V<sup>5+</sup> and V<sup>4+</sup>.
questions.hint: The catalyst metal here is vanadium.

MnO<sub>2</sub> is used to catalyse the decomposition of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and KClO<sub>3</sub>, not the Contact process.
CuO is not the catalyst used in the Contact process.

questions.topic: Applications of d- & f-Block Elements
questions.question: The Haber process for ammonia synthesis uses which catalyst?
options: Ni
Fe (promoted with Mo)
Pt
Cr
questions.explanation: Finely divided iron, promoted with molybdenum, is the standard industrial catalyst for the Haber process.
questions.hint: This is the same metal that forms the bulk of structural steel.
distractor_logic: Ni is used to catalyse hydrogenation reactions, not the Haber process.
Pt is used in catalytic converters and some oxidation reactions, not the Haber process.
Cr is not the standard catalyst for ammonia synthesis.

questions.topic: Applications of d- & f-Block Elements
questions.question: Ziegler–Natta catalysts, used in alkene polymerisation, are based on:
options: KMnO<sub>4</sub> and NaOH
TiCl<sub>4</sub> and an aluminium alkyl
V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> and Pt
K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

questions.hint: The transition metal component here is titanium.
distractor_logic: KMnO<sub>4</sub> and NaOH are not used as a Ziegler–Natta catalyst system.
V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> and Pt are catalysts for other processes, not alkene polymerisation of this type.
K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> form an oxidising mixture, unrelated to Ziegler–Natta catalysis.

questions.topic: Applications of d- & f-Block Elements
questions.question: Mischmetal, used in lighter flints, is primarily an alloy of:
options: Actinoids
Lanthanoids
Alkali metals
Noble gases
questions.explanation: Mischmetal is a pyrophoric alloy rich in lanthanoid metals (mainly Ce, La and Nd) combined with a little iron.
questions.hint: This alloy is drawn from the f-block series that is not radioactive as a whole.
distractor_logic: Actinoids are radioactive and not the basis of the everyday mischmetal alloy used in flints.
Alkali metals are far too reactive with air/moisture to be used this way and are not part of mischmetal.
Noble gases do not form alloys at all.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Cu (Z=29) has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> as an atom, yet Cu<sup>2+</sup> is classed as a typical transition ion. What is the configuration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> and why does it justify this classification?
options: [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>; the d subshell is partially filled
[Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>; the d subshell is fully filled
[Ar]4s<sup>1</sup>; only the s electron remains
[Ar]3d<sup>8</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>; one d and one s electron remain
questions.explanation: Cu<sup>2+</sup> forms by removing the 4s electron and one 3d electron, giving [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>, which has a partially filled d subshell and so is a typical transition ion despite the neutral atom's d<sup>10</sup> configuration.
questions.hint: Removing two electrons from Cu means losing the single 4s electron plus one from the d subshell.
distractor_logic: A fully-filled d<sup>10</sup> ion would be Cu<sup>+</sup>, formed by removing only the 4s electron, not Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
Removing electrons from a transition metal ion always empties the outer s subshell first and completely, never leaving an s electron behind while d electrons are also removed.
This configuration accounts for only 9 electrons removed relative to Cu<sup>0</sup>'s 3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>, which is inconsistent with forming a 2+ ion by losing exactly two electrons.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Which statement correctly explains why Sc is sometimes regarded as not being a typical transition element, despite lying in the d-block?
options: Sc metal is a non-metal, unlike other transition elements
Sc's only common ion, Sc<sup>3+</sup>, has a d<sup>0</sup> configuration with no d electrons at all
Sc has two stable oxidation states, +2 and +4
Sc does not form any compounds
questions.explanation: Although the Sc atom itself is [Ar]3d<sup>1</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, its only significant ion, Sc<sup>3+</sup>, is [Ar] with no d electrons (d<sup>0</sup>), so by the ion-based definition it is atypical.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the single d electron when scandium forms its usual ion.
distractor_logic: Sc is very much a metal, with typical metallic lustre and conductivity.
Sc's dominant and essentially only common oxidation state is +3, not +2 or +4.
Sc forms many compounds, such as Sc<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and ScCl<sub>3</sub>; this statement is false.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: Palladium (Pd, Z=46) has the unusual ground-state configuration [Kr]4d<sup>10</sup>5s<sup>0</sup>, skipping the 5s subshell entirely. This is best explained by:
options: A simple typographical convention with no physical basis
The extra stability associated with a completely filled 4d<sup>10</sup> subshell
Pd having no electrons beyond the krypton core
Pd being an f-block element
questions.explanation: As with Cr and Cu, a fully-filled d subshell provides extra stability, and in Pd's case both 5s electrons move into 4d to achieve d<sup>10</sup>s<sup>0</sup>.
questions.hint: This is the same underlying stability effect seen with Cr and Cu, just taken further.
distractor_logic: This is a genuine physical effect of electron configuration stability, not merely a notational quirk.
Pd has 10 electrons beyond the krypton core (all in 4d), not zero.
Pd is squarely in the 4d transition series (d-block), not the f-block.

questions.topic: Position of d- & f-Block Elements & Electronic Configuration
questions.question: A student claims: 'Since La is placed with the lanthanoids in the periodic table, it must have at least one 4f electron.' Is this claim correct?
options: Yes, La is [Xe]4f<sup>1</sup>5d<sup>0</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>
No, La is [Xe]5d<sup>1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup> with zero 4f electrons; it is placed there only by convention
Yes, because all elements in a periodic table row must share the same subshell being filled
No, because La actually belongs to the actinoid series
questions.explanation: La has the configuration [Xe]5d<sup>1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>, with no electrons in 4f at all; it heads the lanthanoid row purely as a matter of periodic-table convention, not because of its own configuration.
questions.hint: Recall which two elements are placed at the head of the f-block despite having zero f electrons themselves.
distractor_logic: This configuration is actually that of Ce, not La; La itself has no 4f electron.
Elements placed together for convenience (like La with the lanthanoids) need not share identical subshell filling.
La belongs with the lanthanoids, not the actinoids, by periodic table position.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Across the 3d series, atomic radius falls from Sc to about the middle of the series but levels off and rises slightly from Fe/Co toward Cu/Zn. What causes this partial reversal?
options: Nuclear charge starts decreasing from Fe onward
Electron-electron repulsion among the increasing number of d electrons begins to outweigh the effect of rising nuclear charge
The 4s subshell becomes completely empty from Fe onward
Radioactive decay changes the atomic number of these elements
questions.explanation: As d-electron count rises past the midpoint, repulsion between them increasingly offsets the pull of the growing nuclear charge, so the radius contraction slows and slightly reverses.
questions.hint: Consider what happens as more electrons crowd into the same d subshell.
distractor_logic: Nuclear charge (number of protons) increases steadily across the whole period; it never decreases.
The 4s subshell remains occupied (typically 4s<sup>2</sup>) for most of these later elements, not empty.
None of these are radioactive under normal conditions; radioactive decay is irrelevant here.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Nb (4d series) and Ta (5d series) are notoriously difficult to separate chemically. Using the concept of lanthanoid contraction, explain why.
options: Nb and Ta have completely different electronic configurations
The lanthanoid contraction preceding Ta almost cancels the expected radius increase from Nb to Ta, making their sizes and chemistry very similar
Nb and Ta are actually the same element with different names
Ta has a much smaller radius than Nb because of its higher group number
questions.explanation: As with Zr/Hf, the lanthanide contraction inserted before the 5d series nearly offsets the size increase expected on descending a group, leaving Nb and Ta with almost identical radii and properties.
questions.hint: This is the same reasoning used for the classic Zr/Hf pair.
distractor_logic: Nb and Ta have analogous, closely related configurations (not 'completely different'), which is actually part of why they behave so similarly.
Nb and Ta are distinct elements with different atomic numbers, just chemically very similar.
Ta's radius is close to, not much smaller than, Nb's; the contraction nearly cancels the expected group-descent increase rather than causing a decrease.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: Which of the following correctly ranks these three metals by increasing enthalpy of atomisation, consistent with the trend of transition metals peaking near the middle of a series?
options: Zn < V < W
W < V < Zn
Zn < W < V
V < Zn < W
questions.explanation: Enthalpy of atomisation tends to be highest for metals with a larger number of unpaired d electrons available for metallic bonding (typically groups 5-6, e.g. V, W) and lowest for metals with a completed d<sup>10</sup> shell like Zn.
questions.hint: Which of these three has a fully-filled d subshell, and which are from the middle of a transition series known for very high melting/atomisation enthalpies?
distractor_logic: This places W below V, but tungsten's exceptionally strong metallic bonding gives it one of the very highest atomisation enthalpies of any metal, well above V.
This places Zn between W and V, but Zn's completed d<sup>10</sup> shell makes its atomisation enthalpy the lowest of the three, not intermediate.
This places Zn above V, but Zn's atomisation enthalpy is the lowest of the three due to its filled d<sup>10</sup> configuration.

questions.topic: General Trends – Atomic & Ionic Radii, Metallic Character
questions.question: A textbook states that 'transition metals show far higher enthalpies of atomisation than s-block metals such as Na or Ca.' What is the best explanation for this?
options: Transition metals have larger atomic radii than s-block metals
Both ns and (n−1)d electrons participate in the metallic bonding of transition metals, giving stronger interatomic attraction
s-block metals are non-metals and do not form metallic bonds
Transition metals have lower melting points than s-block metals
questions.explanation: Because both the outer ns electrons and the inner (n−1)d electrons contribute to the 'electron sea', transition metals experience stronger metallic bonding and hence higher atomisation enthalpies.
questions.hint: Compare how many types of electrons contribute to the metallic bond in each case.
distractor_logic: Transition metals are generally smaller, not larger, than the alkali/alkaline earth metals of the same period, which is the opposite of what would explain higher atomisation enthalpy via size.
s-block metals are indeed metals and do form metallic bonds; this statement is false.
Transition metals actually have higher, not lower, melting points than most s-block metals, consistent with stronger bonding.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: The first ionization enthalpy of Zn is higher than that of Cu, even though Zn follows Cu in the series. What explains this apparent 'anomaly'?
options: Zn has a smaller nuclear charge than Cu
Zn's electron is removed from a stable, fully-filled 3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> configuration, which resists ionization more than Cu's single 4s electron
Zn has fewer protons than Cu, reducing the pull on its electrons
Cu's 3d subshell is only half filled, making its electrons easier to remove
questions.explanation: Zn's outer electron is removed from a doubly-stable filled d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> arrangement, which is harder to disturb, giving Zn a higher IE<sub>1</sub> than expected from a simple smooth trend.
questions.hint: Compare the type of configuration each metal loses its first electron from.
distractor_logic: Zn (Z=30) has one more proton than Cu (Z=29), a higher, not lower, nuclear charge.
This reverses the actual relationship; Zn has more protons than Cu, not fewer.
Cu's 3d subshell is fully filled (3d<sup>10</sup>), not half-filled; the half-filled configuration example in this series is Cr, not Cu.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: Mn shows oxidation states ranging from +2 to +7, more than any other 3d metal. In MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, what is the oxidation state of Mn, and how is it consistent with its electronic configuration?
options: +2, using only the 4s electrons
+7, using all five 3d and both 4s electrons
+5, using three 3d electrons only
+7, but this cannot be explained by its configuration
questions.explanation: Mn is [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>; formally involving all seven of these outer electrons in bonding, as in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, gives the maximum oxidation state of +7.
questions.hint: Add up all the electrons manganese has beyond its noble-gas core.
distractor_logic: +2 corresponds to loss of only the two 4s electrons, not the +7 state asked about.
+5 would involve only some of the outer electrons; it is not the oxidation state of Mn in permanganate.
+7 is fully explained by Mn's configuration, since 5 (3d) + 2 (4s) = 7 electrons are formally involved.

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: Compare the highest common oxidation states of V, Cr and Mn. Which correctly matches each element to its highest common oxidation state and configuration-based reasoning?
options: V: +5 (3d<sup>3</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, 5 electrons); Cr: +6 (3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>, 6 electrons); Mn: +7 (3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, 7 electrons)
V: +3; Cr: +3; Mn: +3, since +3 is always the maximum for 3d metals
V: +5; Cr: +5; Mn: +5, since these three elements behave identically
questions.explanation: The maximum oxidation state tracks the number of electrons beyond the argon core: V (5 electrons) → +5, Cr (6 electrons) → +6, Mn (7 electrons) → +7, a steadily rising pattern across this stretch of the series.
questions.hint: Count the total 3d + 4s electrons for each element and see how that number relates to its highest oxidation state.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct assignments; V does not reach +7, and Mn does not stop at +5.
+3 is a common, but not the maximum, oxidation state for these particular elements; V, Cr and Mn all exceed +3.
These three elements do not behave identically; their maximum oxidation states differ (+5, +6, +7 respectively).

questions.topic: General Trends – Ionization Enthalpy & Oxidation States
questions.question: Beyond Mn, the maximum oxidation states of Fe, Co, Ni, Cu and Zn drop sharply, with +2/+3 dominating. What is the best explanation?
options: These elements have fewer total electrons than Mn
Increasing nuclear charge holds the d-electrons more tightly, making it energetically unfavourable to remove all of them
These elements are not part of the transition series
These elements have no electrons in the 4s subshell at all
questions.explanation: As nuclear charge rises past Mn, the d-electrons are bound more strongly, so the energy cost of removing many of them to reach a very high oxidation state outweighs the benefit, and lower states (+2, +3) become dominant instead.
questions.hint: Think about how increasing nuclear charge affects the ease of removing many d-electrons at once.
distractor_logic: Fe, Co, Ni, Cu and Zn actually have equal or more total electrons than Mn, not fewer.
These are all firmly part of the 3d transition series.
These elements do have 4s electrons (e.g. Fe is 3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>); the 4s subshell is not empty.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Given that E°(Zn<sup>2+</sup>/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V, predict what happens when a strip of zinc metal is placed in a solution of copper sulfate.
options: No reaction occurs because both are transition metals
Zn is oxidised to Zn<sup>2+</sup> while Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu metal, which deposits on the zinc strip
Cu metal dissolves further into solution as Cu<sup>2+</sup>
Zn<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Zn while Cu is oxidised
questions.explanation: Since E°(Zn<sup>2+</sup>/Zn) is more negative than E°(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu), Zn is the better reducing agent: it is spontaneously oxidised while Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced and deposits as copper metal.
questions.hint: Compare the two electrode potentials to see which metal is more easily oxidised.
distractor_logic: Zinc is not a transition element in the typical sense, but more importantly the large potential difference between the two half-cells drives a spontaneous reaction.
Cu<sup>2+</sup>, being the more easily reduced species, is deposited as metal rather than Cu dissolving further.
This reverses the correct direction of electron flow; Zn is oxidised (loses electrons) and Zn<sup>2+</sup>, not Zn, is the product on that side.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Fe has E°(Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe) = −0.44 V, a less negative value than expected from a simple trend based on atomic size alone. Which combination of factors best accounts for the observed E° values across the 3d series?
options: Colour of the ion alone
The combined effect of atomisation enthalpy, ionization enthalpy and hydration enthalpy of the ion
Radioactive half-life of the isotope
Position of the element in the periodic table alone, with no reference to any enthalpy terms
questions.explanation: E° values reflect a thermodynamic cycle involving atomisation, ionization and hydration enthalpies together, which is why the trend across the series is irregular rather than a simple function of radius or position.
questions.hint: Recall the three-part thermodynamic cycle used to rationalise electrode potentials.
distractor_logic: The colour of an ion has no thermodynamic connection to its electrode potential.
None of the 3d metals are radioactive under normal conditions; this is irrelevant.
Position alone does not determine E°; the actual determining factors are the specific enthalpy terms in the cycle.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: Both Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) and Zn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>10</sup>) have more negative E° values than a simple smooth trend would predict from their position. What do these two cases have in common?
options: Both ions have unusually large ionic radii
Both ions have extra-stable electronic configurations (half-filled or fully-filled d subshell), making oxidation of the metal comparatively favourable
Both elements are non-metals
Both ions are strongly coloured
questions.explanation: Forming Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) or Zn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>10</sup>) reaches an especially stable configuration, so oxidation of the parent metal is comparatively easy, giving both a more negative E° than their neighbours.
questions.hint: Think about what these two particular d-electron counts have in common in terms of stability.
distractor_logic: Ionic radius is not the property linking these two cases; the shared feature is electronic stability.
Both Mn and Zn are firmly metals, not non-metals.
Zn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>10</sup>) is actually colourless, so 'strongly coloured' does not apply to both ions.

questions.topic: Standard Electrode Potentials & Chemical Reactivity
questions.question: A student mixes dilute HCl with copper turnings and observes no visible reaction, then repeats the experiment with iron filings and observes vigorous gas evolution. Explain this difference using standard electrode potentials.
options: Fe and Cu have identical electrode potentials, so the difference must be due to particle size only
Fe has a negative E° (favouring oxidation by H<sup>+</sup>) while Cu has a positive E° (H<sup>+</sup> cannot oxidise it)
Copper reacts faster than iron with all acids
Hydrochloric acid does not contain any H<sup>+</sup> ions
questions.explanation: Fe's negative E° means H<sup>+</sup> can oxidise it, releasing H<sub>2</sub> gas, whereas Cu's positive E° means H<sup>+</sup> cannot oxidise Cu under these conditions, so no reaction is observed.
questions.hint: Compare the sign of each metal's standard reduction potential.
distractor_logic: Fe and Cu have very different electrode potentials (−0.44 V vs +0.34 V), so particle size is not the deciding factor here.
This reverses the actual outcome; it is iron, not copper, that reacts readily with dilute HCl.
Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid that fully dissociates to give H<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions in solution.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (high-spin, 3d<sup>6</sup>, 4 unpaired electrons) and state whether the ion is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
options: μ = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM; paramagnetic
μ = 0 BM; diamagnetic
μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM; paramagnetic
μ = √8 ≈ 2.83 BM; diamagnetic
questions.explanation: With n = 4 unpaired electrons, μ = √4(4+2) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM; since n > 0, Fe<sup>2+</sup> is paramagnetic.
questions.hint: Substitute n = 4 into the spin-only formula.
distractor_logic: μ = 0 would require zero unpaired electrons, which describes a d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> ion, not high-spin Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
√35 corresponds to n = 5 unpaired electrons (as in Mn<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>5</sup>), not the n = 4 case of Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
This value uses n = 2, not n = 4, and any non-zero magnetic moment indicates paramagnetism, not diamagnetism.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
questions.question: Sc<sup>3+</sup>, Ti<sup>4+</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> are all colourless in aqueous solution, while Fe<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Mn<sup>2+</sup> are coloured. What single structural feature explains this pattern?
options: The colourless ions all have a d<sup>0</sup> or d<sup>10</sup> configuration, so no d-d transition is possible
The colourless ions have larger ionic radii than the coloured ones
The colourless ions are all negatively charged
The coloured ions are all radioactive
questions.explanation: Sc<sup>3+</sup> and Ti<sup>4+</sup> are d<sup>0</sup>, and Zn<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>10</sup>; with no partially filled d subshell, no d-d transition can occur, so these ions are colourless, unlike the partially-filled-d coloured ions.
questions.hint: Check the d-electron count of each colourless ion.
distractor_logic: Ionic radius has no direct bearing on whether d-d transitions, and hence colour, are possible.
All the ions listed are actually cations (positively charged), not negatively charged.
None of these common ions are radioactive; radioactivity is unrelated to their colour.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties, Colour & Catalytic Behaviour
